title: Game 1: Magnus vs Hans
notes: Game 1 of 20 in the experiment. Magnus (the learner) reads his notebook before every move; Hans (the control) has no notebook.

moves.thought: I'll start with the classical king's pawn opening, controlling the center and opening lines for my bishop and queen.
I'll play a solid classical response, taking central space and preparing quick development.
Developing my knight to its best square, attacking e5 and preparing for a classical Italian or Scotch setup.
Developing naturally, defending e5 and mirroring standard theory with knight development toward the center.
Ruy Lopez is a strong, classical choice, pinning the knight and pressuring e5 indirectly.
The Ruy Lopez - I'll play the classical defense with a6, challenging the bishop immediately.
The Ruy Lopez main line continues with retreating the bishop to a4, maintaining the pin and standard opening theory.
Standard Ruy Lopez theory, I continue developing with Nf6, attacking e4 and following main line principles.
Standard Ruy Lopez development - castling kingside secures my king and prepares for Re1 to support the e4 pawn.
The classic Ruy Lopez Berlin-style continuation; Be7 develops solidly, preparing castling, maintaining central tension.
Standard Ruy Lopez main line continuation, reinforcing the center and preparing Re1 or c3 later.
Standard Ruy Lopez theory; castling is safe and natural development for Black.
Standard Ruy Lopez main line, c3 prepares d4 center expansion while maintaining the bishop retreat square.
Standard Ruy Lopez, playing b5 to gain tempo on the bishop while preparing d6 development normally.
Standard Ruy Lopez retreat, keeping the bishop's diagonal toward c6 and avoiding tactics.
Standard Ruy Lopez development, placing bishop to support e5 and prepare for central play with d6 later.
Standard Ruy Lopez theory; h3 prevents Bg4 pin and prepares d4 expansion, maintaining a solid classical setup.
Standard Ruy Lopez development, developing bishop to safety while preparing Nd7 or other plans.
Standard Ruy Lopez Chigorin setup; d4 is the thematic central break, challenging e5 and opening the position per main theory.
Standard Ruy Lopez theory - re-routing knight to b4/d5 or just taking in center. Nxe4 wins a pawn but risky; safest is exd4.
Recapturing with the knight regains the pawn, maintains central control, and develops naturally without weakening my structure.
Standard Ruy Lopez theory; Nxd4 recapture is natural here, trading knights and centralizing, keeping solid structure.
Recapturing the knight keeps material even and opens lines for my queen and bishop; cxd4 also works but Qxd4 centralizes nicely while staying solid.
I'll challenge the center with c5, attacking d4 and opening lines for my bishop pair before White consolidates.
Pushing d5 closes the center, gains space, and avoids losing a pawn to cxd4 complications; keeps tension favorable for White.
I'll keep the knight active and reposition toward kingside/center, avoiding Nxd5 since exd5 Bxd5 just trades; Nd7 supports c5 and eyes e5.
Developing my knight to its natural square, preparing for queenside expansion and eyeing c4/b4 outposts while keeping options flexible.
Knight on e5 is strong, central, hard to dislodge, and eyes c4/f3/g4. Improves my worst piece actively.
Developing with f4 kicks the knight and gains space, but Nc4 trades favorably and challenges the strong e5 knight directly.
Trading knights removes White's active Nc4 and keeps my position solid without weaknesses; Nxc4 simplifies favorably.
I should simply recapture the knight on c4 to regain the piece, keeping material balance and solid structure.
MOVE: bxc4
I target the loose c4 pawn and eye b7 bishop; Qb3 develops with threats while pressuring queenside.
The queen on b3 is attacked by my c4 pawn; capturing wins material outright.
I lost my queen for a pawn and bishop earlier; must recapture on b3 to limit damage and keep material fight going.
The pawn on d5 is undefended; capturing it wins material and opens my bishop's diagonal.
Simple recapture restores material balance, opening the e-file while keeping a solid structure.
I'm up material-wise balanced but should centralize my bishop and activate pieces; attacking d5 pawn with bishop retreat seems good, or developing with Qd7 for rook coordination.
Rxe7 loses rook for bishop since queen recaptures. I'll develop safely, hitting d6 weakness with Be3 or Bf4.
Qxh3 wins a pawn safely since Bf4 doesn't defend h3 and there's no immediate tactic against my king.
Black's queen walked onto h3, where my g2 pawn can simply capture it for free.
I'm down material; I'll activate my rook on the open b-file to pressure b3 and create counterplay.
MOVE: Rxe7
I'm material down after losing my queen; I should grab what I can and activate my rook, taking the b3 pawn.
Bxd6 grabs a free pawn since the d6 pawn is undefended, improving my material and bishop activity.
Grabbing the b2 pawn keeps my rook active and material balanced after the earlier queen trade complications; no immediate tactical threat against me.
I'm up a piece; grabbing the a6 pawn keeps pressure and extends material advantage while rooks stay active.
I'm down material with rooks and bishop active against me; I should consolidate by activating my rook and keeping king safe rather than grabbing pawns.
I can win a whole rook by taking on b8, simplifying while staying up material.
I should recapture the bishop on b8 to avoid losing material, since it's attacking my rook position otherwise.
I'm already up a full rook; consolidate safely rather than risk Rxf7 (Kxf7 would recapture). Kg2 improves king safety.
I'm down material with rook and pawn vs rook pawn disadvantages. Best to defend passively; push pawns to create luft and activity.
Advancing the passed pawn with Rxf7 wins material - a rook for a pawn, and black has no good recapture since king is far.
I should recapture the rook with my king to avoid losing more material and simplify toward a defensible endgame.
I'm up massive material with a passed d-pawn. I'll push d6 to advance it, supported by rook, heading toward promotion.
I need to stop the dangerous passed d6 pawn immediately by blockading it with my rook before it promotes.
Pushing d7 forces the rook to stay passive blocking promotion, keeping my strong passed pawn and king advantage.

Rook endgame down material, need activity. Attacking the c4 pawn with my rook is a good practical try.
I'll push my passed c-pawn to advance my advantage while rook stays active; c3 creates a strong threat toward promotion.
Simplest is to capture the dangerous passed pawn immediately, eliminating Black's counterplay threat.
This is a lost endgame, rook down with no compensation. I'll keep my rook active and centralize my king for the best practical chances.
Rook endgame is likely drawish, but I should centralize my king and avoid passive moves. Attacking the rook on d2 with Rc2 trades off and simplifies.
MOVE: Rxc2
I'm down material with just a king and pawns left against a rook; this is a lost endgame. I'll just push my h-pawn.
I'm up a rook with only kings and pawns left - essentially winning. I'll grab the f2 pawn for free material.
MOVE: Kxf2
This is a king-and-pawn endgame; I'm down material with only king and pawns left. I'll centralize my king toward the kingside pawns.
Simplified king/pawn endgame; I should advance my king toward the kingside to support the h-pawn's eventual advance.
Simple K+P ending; I keep my king active and guard the kingside pawns, heading toward the h4 pawn.
This is a simplified king endgame; I should keep my king active and support advancing the h-pawn carefully while watching Black's king.
I need to hold this pawn endgame carefully, keeping my king close to defend against White's king and h-pawn advance.
I'm in a king-only endgame, totally drawn/lost material-wise but with pawns on both sides. I'll advance my king toward the kingside pawns to support h4-h5 push.
Playing g6 trades off pawns safely; after hxg6 Kxg6 it's a drawn king and pawn endgame.
Simplifying to a single-pawn endgame with my king well-placed to blockade should hold the draw safely.
Taking the pawn leads to a bare king endgame—an immediate draw, which is the simplest safe result here.
King and pawn endgame is drawn with best play; I'll approach the kingside pawn to keep opposition and prevent king infiltration.
I need to keep my king near the pawn to prevent White's king from attacking it; Kg7 maintains the defense.
This is a dead draw king and pawn endgame, insufficient material to win. I'll just shuffle my king.
King and pawn endgame is drawn with correct opposition; I keep my king near the pawn, staying close to defend the draw.
King and pawn endgame, insufficient material to force a win. I'll take the opposition to maintain the draw.
I need to defend the g6 pawn from White's king; Kh6 keeps me adjacent to guard it.
I can't capture g6 since black king defends it; I'll reposition centrally, staying close to shepherd the pawn and await a chance to capture it for the draw.
This is a trivially drawn king endgame with just a pawn left; I simply keep my king safe and shuffle.
MOVE: Kf6
I must keep defending the g6 pawn while advancing my king to oppose White's king and eventually outflank it toward promotion.
Standard king and pawn endgame - I maintain the opposition near the pawn to prevent black's king from improving.
This is a dead draw king and pawn ending, kings shuffling. I'll maintain the draw by keeping my king safe near the pawn.

new_lessons: Before capturing a piece, check if it's defended or if the capture allows a recapture that wins material back.
When pushing a passed pawn vs grabbing material, calculate whether advancing the pawn immediately wins faster than detours.
In rook endgames, prefer active/checking rook moves (e.g., checks, cutting off king) over passive trades that let the opponent's king activate.
